Now let me compile the verse-by-verse notes from all the sources I've gathered.

# 1 Peter 4 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview

1 Peter 4 continues the theme of suffering for righteousness that began in 3:13. Peter exhorts believers to adopt Christ's mindset toward suffering, break decisively with the sinful past, love one another fervently in light of the approaching end, exercise spiritual gifts, and — most extensively — endure persecution with joy, distinguishing between suffering for Christ and suffering for wrongdoing. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-4/; https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/1-peter/)

---

## v. 4:1 — "Therefore, since Christ suffered in His body, arm yourselves with the same resolve, because anyone who has suffered in his body is done with sin."

The "therefore" reaches back primarily to 1 Peter 3:18 ("Christ also suffered for sins … being put to death in the flesh"). Peter draws a practical conclusion: Christ's suffering is not only atoning but exemplary. Believers are to "arm" themselves — a military metaphor (Greek *hoplisasthe*, from *hoplon* = heavy weaponry) implying that the Christian life is a battle requiring the heaviest armour available. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1peter_verse_by_verse_41-9; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-4/)

The word translated "resolve" (Greek *ennoia*) is better rendered "mind," "way of thinking," or "attitude." Ellicott notes it does not merely mean "put yourselves into the same disposition" but rather "with the same conception" — the view Christ took of suffering itself as a shield in the day of trial. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-peter-4.html)

"Anyone who has suffered in his body is done with sin": This does not teach sinless perfection. D. Edmond Hiebert (cited in Enduring Word) explains that it "depicts the spiritual state of the victorious sufferer … his old life, dominated by the power of sin, has been terminated." Grudem adds, "Whoever has suffered for doing right, and has still gone on obeying God in spite of the suffering it involved, has made a clear break with sin." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-4/)

**Reformed reading (Ligonier / Sproul influence):** Ligonier notes that Jesus, though sinless, "ceased from sin" by refusing to give in to temptation and by fulfilling the Father's will even to death. Believers united with Christ share in that death to sin — though complete cessation from sin awaits glory. John Calvin is cited: "if we are united to Christ 'we are really and effectually supplied with invincible weapons to subdue the flesh.'" (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/arm-yourselves)

**Baptist reading (Spurgeon):** Spurgeon (cited at Precept Austin) says, "Brethren, we have a Savior who suffered for us. As the Head was, such must the members expect to be … inasmuch as we suffered in him, yea, and died in him, we ought to reckon that we are henceforth dead to sin." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1peter_verse_by_verse_41-9)

Ellicott notes the thought derives from Romans 6:7 and that for the redeemed, death of the body puts a stop to further possibility of sin. The Greek verb *pepautai* means "hath been caused to rest" — a pause imposed from without, not merely a voluntary cessation. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-peter-4.html)

---

## v. 4:2 — "Consequently, he does not live out his remaining time on earth for human passions, but for the will of God."

The break with sin reorients the believer's entire remaining life. Peter gives two time-markers: "no longer" (looking back at the old life now renounced) and "the rest of his time" (looking forward to days lived for God's will). David Guzik notes that every temptation should be answered with "no longer," while every day given by God will require an account. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-4/)

Precept Austin emphasises that the motivation for holiness flows from Christ's sufferings (1 Pet 3:18) and His imminent return to judge (v.5). The believer is no longer driven by "human passions" (*anthrōpōn epithymiais*) but lives for God's will — a complete reorientation of life's purpose. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1peter_verse_by_verse_41-9)

---

## v. 4:3 — "For you have spent enough time in the past carrying out the same desires as the Gentiles: living in debauchery, lust, drunkenness, orgies, carousing, and detestable idolatry."

Peter lists six specific sins characteristic of the Gentile world: debauchery (Gk. *aselgeia* — living without moral restraint, especially sexual), lusts, drunkenness, orgies (*kōmoi* — riotous feasting), carousing (*potoi* — drinking parties), and detestable idolatry. Hiebert notes *aselgeia* "denotes excesses of all kinds of evil … an inordinate indulgence of appetites to the extent of violating a sense of public decency." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-4/)

Precept Austin notes that the list demonstrates how little fallen humanity has changed in 2,000 years. Peter's point is that believers "have spent enough time" (*arketos … chronos*) — implying deliberate sufficiency: the past was quite enough; now it is time to live differently. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1peter_verse_by_verse_41-9)

---

## v. 4:4 — "Because of this, they consider it strange of you not to plunge with them into the same flood of reckless indiscretion, and they heap abuse on you."

Former companions are "surprised" (Gk. *xenizontai* — they find it foreign, strange) that believers no longer join their lifestyle. The phrase "flood of reckless indiscretion" (or "flood of dissipation" — *tēn autēn tēs asōtias anachusin*) depicts sin as a torrent of wastefulness. Guzik notes: "If life lived after the flesh is anything, it is a waste." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-4/)

The slander ("heap abuse," literally "blaspheme") arises because holy living convicts the consciences of the ungodly. F.B. Meyer is cited: "It does not matter how your good deeds are received by men. If you are like God, you will find them received with contempt and ingratitude." Best (cited in Hiebert) adds that since pagan religious ceremonies were woven into civic and social life, Christians had to withdraw far more radically than modern readers may appreciate. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-4/)

---

## v. 4:5 — "But they will have to give an account to Him who is ready to judge the living and the dead."

The slanderers will not escape. God is "ready" (*hetoimōs echonti*) to judge — the present tense suggests ongoing readiness. This verse provides comfort for the persecuted: ultimate justice belongs to God, and He will judge both "the living and the dead." Guzik comments that this is a sober reminder that those who live by the world's rules will see their lives as a waste when measured against eternity. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-4/)

---

## v. 4:6 — "That is why the gospel was preached even to those who are now dead, so that they might be judged as men in the flesh, but live according to God in the spirit."

This is one of the most difficult verses in the epistle. The Pulpit Commentary calls the passage "the most difficult in the entire Epistle." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/1_peter/4.htm)

**Three main interpretations** (summarised from John Piper at Desiring God):

1. **The "Descent" view:** Christ, between His death and resurrection, went to the realm of the dead (Hades/Sheol) and preached the gospel to Old Testament saints, leading them to heaven. Linked to Ephesians 4:8 ("He led captivity captive") and the "spirits in prison" of 3:19. Piper notes this is the "traditional view" but finds it odd that the focus would be limited to those disobedient in Noah's day.

2. **The "Victory Proclamation" view:** Christ's "preaching" was His ascended proclamation of victory over fallen angels ("the spirits in prison" of 3:19 are evil angels). Again, Piper finds the connection to Noah's day hard to follow.

3. **The "Preaching through Noah" view:** Christ in His Spirit preached through Noah to the generation of the flood. Those who disobeyed are now "spirits in prison." This fits 1 Peter 1:10-11, where the "Spirit of Christ" was in the Old Testament prophets. Piper leans toward this view. (https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/do-unbelievers-get-a-second-chance-after-death)

**Standard evangelical reading (GotQuestions.org / NET Bible sense):** "Those who are now dead" refers to believers who heard the gospel *while alive* but have since died — possibly martyrs. Though they were "judged in the flesh" (suffered physical death), they now "live in the spirit" (enjoy eternal life with God). This reading preserves the clear biblical teaching that there is no second chance after death (Heb 9:27). The NIV inserts "now" before "dead" to clarify this sense. (https://www.gotquestions.org/gospel-preached-to-those-who-are-dead.html)

**Reformed reading (StudyLight summary):** Of 80 commentators surveyed, the text divides six ways. The dominant Reformed (Calvinist) view is that the gospel was preached to people when they were alive, who are now dead — not a post-mortem evangelism. Lenski states: "Peter does not say that the gospel is being preached even to the dead but was preached." (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-peter/4-6.html)

**Lutheran reading:** Martin Luther famously said of this passage: "A wonderful text is this, and a more obscure passage perhaps than any other in the New Testament, so that I do not know for a certainty just what Peter means." (https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/do-unbelievers-get-a-second-chance-after-death)

**Enduring Word (Pentecostal/charismatic):** Guzik holds that during Christ's descent He "preached a message of salvation to the faithful dead in Abraham's Bosom (Luke 16:22) who anticipated the work of the Messiah for them." This was "not the offer of a second chance, but the completion of the salvation of those who had been faithful to God under their first chance." He also allows that Peter may have had Christian martyrs in view. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-4/)

---

## v. 4:7 — "The end of all things is near. Therefore be clear-minded and sober, so that you can pray."

"The end of all things is near" (Gk. *pantōn de to telos ēngiken*): "End" (*telos*) means consummation, the goal toward which history moves — not annihilation but fulfilment of God's purposes. Precept Austin provides extensive lexical analysis showing *telos* refers to "the end of the age" and the return of Christ. The perfect tense *ēngiken* ("has drawn near") conveys imminence — it can break in at any time. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1_peter_47-13)

"Clear-minded" (*sōphronēsate*) and "sober" (*nēpsate*) are both aorist imperatives — urgent commands for self-controlled, watchful living. The purpose clause "so that you can pray" (*eis proseuchas*) shows that prayer is the specific goal: in light of the approaching end, prayer becomes supremely important. Guzik laments that many who believe Jesus is coming soon based on prophecy charts fail to apply that belief by becoming more diligent in prayer. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-4/)

---

## v. 4:8 — "Above all, love one another deeply, because love covers over a multitude of sins."

"Above all" (*pro pantōn*) signals the pre-eminence of love among Christian duties. "Deeply" translates *ektenē* — "fervently," "stretched-out," a word suggesting earnest, sustained effort, not fleeting emotion. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-4/)

"Love covers over a multitude of sins": This echoes Proverbs 10:12. Grudem explains: "Where love abounds in a fellowship of Christians, many small offences, and even some large ones, are readily overlooked and forgotten. But where love is lacking, every word is viewed with suspicion … and conflicts abound — to Satan's perverse delight." The saying does not mean love atones for sin (only Christ's blood does that), but that love refuses to expose or dwell on the faults of others. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-4/)

---

## v. 4:9 — "Show hospitality to one another without complaining."

Hospitality (*philoxenoi*) — literally "love of strangers" — was a crucial virtue in the early church, when travelling believers and persecuted Christians needed shelter. "Without complaining" (*aneu gongysmou*) is "a frank recognition that the practice of hospitality could become costly, burdensome, and irritating. The Greek term denotes a muttering or low speaking as a sign of displeasure" (Hiebert, cited in Guzik). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-4/)

---

## v. 4:10 — "As good stewards of the manifold grace of God, each of you should use whatever gift he has received to serve one another."

Every believer has received a "gift" (*charisma*) — a gracious endowment from God. These gifts are stewarded, not owned. "Manifold" (*poikilēs*) means "many-coloured" or "variegated" — F.B. Meyer writes: "As when a ray of light breaks into a spray of many hues, so each of us receives God's grace at a different angle, and flashes it back broken up into some fresh colour." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-4/)

Precept Austin notes a deliberate word-link: the "various trials" of 1 Peter 1:6 use the same rare Greek word *poikilos* as the "manifold grace" of 4:10 — God's grace is as varied as the trials it meets. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1_peter_commentaries)

Guzik warns: "If we are bad stewards of the manifold grace of God, it is as if that grace was given to us in vain. That grace is wasted, because it only comes to us and doesn't move through us." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-4/)

---

## v. 4:11 — "If anyone speaks, he should speak as one conveying the words of God. If anyone serves, he should serve with the strength God provides, so that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom be the glory and the power forever and ever. Amen."

Peter divides gifts into two broad categories: speaking and serving. Speaking gifts must be exercised "as one conveying the words of God" (*hōs logia theou*) — with the gravity and faithfulness due to divine oracles, not personal opinion. Serving gifts must rely on "the strength God provides" (*hōs ex ischyos hēs chorēgei ho theos*), not human energy alone. The ultimate goal is that "in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ." The doxology that follows — "to whom be the glory and the power forever and ever. Amen" — may refer to God the Father or to Jesus Christ. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-4/)

---

## v. 4:12 — "Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial that has come upon you, as though something strange were happening to you."

Peter addresses them tenderly as "Beloved" (*agapētoi*) — Sam Storms (TGC) notes this is "designed to remind them that their suffering is no indication of God's displeasure or rejection of them." (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/1-peter/)

"Fiery trial" (*pyrōsei*) literally means "burning" — the metaphor of a smelting furnace where metal is refined. The trial is "for your testing" (*pros peirasmon*). Guzik notes that "Peter once told Jesus to avoid the suffering of the cross (Mark 8:32-33). Once it seemed strange to the Apostle Peter that his Master should think of suffering. Now he thinks it strange that He could have imagined anything else." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-4/)

Precept Austin elaborates: "Christ sits as a refiner before the fire. The metallurgist takes the most pains with the most precious metals … Christ allows us to be subjected to the heat until all of our impurities are burned up … so too Christ can see His own face reflected in our lives." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1_peter_commentaries)

---

## v. 4:13 — "But rejoice that you share in the sufferings of Christ, so that you may be overjoyed at the revelation of His glory."

Rejoicing in suffering is possible because suffering now is a prelude to glory later. "Share in the sufferings of Christ" (*koinōneite tois tou Christou pathēmasin*) does not mean contributing to Christ's atoning work (which is finished), but experiencing the same kind of hostility from the world that He endured, as a consequence of identification with Him (cf. John 15:18-21). (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/1-peter/)

"To the extent" implies a measure: those who have suffered more for Jesus will experience a corresponding depth of joy at His return. Guzik: "We should never deny the place of suffering in building godliness … If suffering was a suitable tool to teach Jesus (Hebrews 5:8), it is a suitable tool to teach His servants." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-4/)

---

## v. 4:14 — "If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the Spirit of glory and of God rests on you."

Being "insulted for the name of Christ" (literally "reproached in Christ's name") brings blessing — echoing Jesus' words in Matthew 5:11-12. "The Spirit of glory and of God rests on you": Precept Austin notes this evokes the Shekinah glory cloud resting on the tabernacle and temple. Today believers are God's temple, and His glory rests upon them — especially when they suffer for Christ. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1peter_verse_by_verse_410-19)

Sam Storms (TGC) offers two possible meanings: either "an extraordinary anointing of the Spirit comes to those who suffer in this manner, in order to energize their endurance," or "the glory yet to come when Christ returns has already entered into their experience ahead of that day." (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/1-peter/)

---

## v. 4:15 — "Indeed, none of you should suffer as a murderer or thief or wrongdoer, or even as a meddler."

Peter draws a sharp distinction: not all suffering is "suffering for Christ." Suffering as a murderer, thief, or wrongdoer is deserved and brings shame. Strikingly, Peter includes "meddler" (*allotriepiskopos* — literally "one who oversees another's affairs," a busybody). Guzik observes: "Such people do suffer a lot of grief and pain, but not for the sake of Jesus." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-4/)

---

## v. 4:16 — "But if you suffer as a Christian, do not be ashamed, but glorify God that you bear that name."

This is one of only three occurrences of the word "Christian" (*Christianos*) in the New Testament (the others being Acts 11:26 and Acts 26:28). Hiebert notes the Latin-derived suffix *-ianos* denotes "a partisan follower" — "members of the Christ-party," not "little Christ" as popularly explained. By the time Peter wrote, the name was widely enough known that one could be persecuted simply for bearing it. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-4/)

Guzik: "Suffering as a Christian is nothing to be ashamed about, even though the world may despise the suffering Christian. Instead, we should glorify God in these matters. We don't glorify God for suffering. But we do glorify Him in suffering, and we glorify Him for what He will accomplish in us and through us with the suffering." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-4/)

---

## v. 4:17 — "For it is time for judgment to begin with the family of God; and if it begins with us, what will the outcome be for those who disobey the gospel of God?"

**The nature of the "judgment":** Sam Storms (TGC, Reformed) makes the critical distinction: "The 'judgment' (*krima*) in view is disciplinary, not punitive, and is designed to refine and sanctify the heart of the believer." Peter uses an *a fortiori* argument (lesser to greater): if God's own children undergo such refining fires now, how much worse will the final outcome be for those who reject the gospel? (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/1-peter/)

Guzik (Enduring Word) echoes this: "Now is our time of fiery trial; the ungodly will have their fire later. The fire we endure now purifies us; the fire the ungodly will endure will punish them. Yet … there is never any punishment from God for us in our sufferings, only purification. For the Christian, the issue of punishment was settled once and for all at the cross." He uses the analogy: the same fire that consumes straw will purify gold. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-4/)

**Baptist reading (Spurgeon, cited by Guzik):** "There is equity in it; for Christians profess to be better than others, and so they ought to be. They say they are regenerate, so they ought to be regenerate. They say that they are a holy people, separated unto Christ; so they ought to be holy, and separate from sinners, as he was." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-4/)

---

## v. 4:18 — "And, 'If it is hard for the righteous to be saved, what will become of the ungodly and the sinner?'"

Peter quotes Proverbs 11:31 (LXX). "Scarcely saved" (or "saved with difficulty") does not mean salvation is earned or uncertain, but that the path of discipleship is arduous — it requires casting away idols and sins. Guzik: "It isn't that our salvation is difficult in the sense of earning it … it is all the free gift of Jesus Christ. Yet our salvation is hard in the sense that the claims of discipleship challenge us." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-4/)

The rhetorical question underscores the terror awaiting those who reject the gospel. If the righteous pass through refining fire, the ungodly face consuming fire.

---

## v. 4:19 — "So then, those who suffer according to God's will should entrust their souls to their faithful Creator and continue to do good."

Peter returns to the theme: suffering must be "according to God's will" (*kata to thelēma tou theou*) — not all suffering qualifies. The response is twofold: (1) entrust (*paratithesthōsan*) one's soul to God, and (2) continue doing good.

The word "entrust" (or "commit") is a banking term for depositing money with a trusted friend — a deposit considered one of the most sacred obligations in ancient life. It is the very word Jesus used on the cross: "Father, into Your hands I commit My spirit" (Luke 23:46). "So when Christians commit their souls to Him, they leave their souls in a safe place." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-4/)

God is described as a "faithful Creator" — combining His sovereignty as Creator (with the right to do as He pleases) with His covenant faithfulness (ensuring He will only do what is ultimately best). Storms (TGC) notes: "Just as Jesus, while suffering, entrusted himself to God, so must believers." (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/1-peter/)

---

## Summary of Key Denominational Differences

### On 1 Peter 4:6 (the gospel preached to the dead):

| Tradition | View |
|-----------|------|
| **Traditional / Pentecostal-charismatic** (Enduring Word) | Christ descended to Abraham's Bosom between death and resurrection, completing the salvation of Old Testament saints; not a second chance but the fulfilment of their first-chance faith. |
| **Reformed Baptist** (John Piper, Desiring God) | Christ in His Spirit preached through Noah to Noah's generation; those who disobeyed are now "spirits in prison." No post-mortem evangelism. |
| **Evangelical** (GotQuestions.org) | "Those who are now dead" = believers who heard the gospel while alive and have since died (martyrs). Though they died physically, they now live spiritually with God. |
| **Lutheran** (Martin Luther) | Luther frankly confessed uncertainty, calling this "a more obscure passage perhaps than any other in the New Testament." |

### On 1 Peter 4:17-18 (judgment beginning with God's house):

Both Reformed (TGC/Sam Storms) and Pentecostal-charismatic (Enduring Word/Guzik) teachers agree the "judgment" is disciplinary/purifying for believers, not punitive — though Guzik draws the application more vividly with the "fire purifies gold, consumes straw" analogy. Sproul's Reformed reading (Ligonier) emphasises God's sovereignty in suffering as part of His providence. Baptist voices (Spurgeon) emphasise the equity and appropriateness of judgment beginning with those who profess holiness.

---

*Sources used: EnduringWord.com (Guzik), PreceptAustin.org, TheGospelCoalition.org (Storms), DesiringGod.org (Piper), GotQuestions.org, Ligonier.org, StudyLight.org (Gill, Ellicott), BibleHub.com (Pulpit Commentary).*
